extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, taxonomists, and students studying freshwater polyzoa (bryozoa), especially Indian fauna
extracted.subtask_description: Provide morphological, anatomical, and ecological diagnostic characters and classification criteria for Polyzoa (Bryozoa), with emphasis on Indian freshwater species, allowing separation of subclasses, orders, families, genera, and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Polyzoa
rubrics_metrics.description: Small coelomate animals, each individual of which consists of a polyp-like organism or polypide enclosed in a 'house' or zooecium composed partly of living tissues. The mouth is surrounded by a circle of ciliated tentacles that can be retracted within the zooecium; the alimentary canal, which is suspended in the zooecium, is Y-shaped and consists of three parts, the oesophagus, the stomach, and the intestine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these core anatomical features (zooecium, retractile tentacular crown, and Y-shaped gut) as primary characters when recognizing or delimiting members of the Polyzoa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclass ENTOPROCTA diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The anus as well as the mouth is enclosed in the circle of tentacles and the zooecium is not very distinctly separated from the polypide. Some forms are solitary or form temporary colonies by budding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of anus inside the tentacular ring and poor separation between zooecium and polypide are key characters; note habitat (mostly marine but a few freshwater/brackish genera).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclass ECTOPROCTA diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The anus is outside the circle of tentacles and the zooecium can always be distinguished from the polypide. All species form by budding permanent communities the individuals in which remain connected together by living tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An external anus and clearly distinct zooecium (and permanent colonial budding) are diagnostic for ectoprocts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order GYMNOLÆMATA diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ectoproctous polyzoa the polypides of which have no epistome; the zooecia are in nearly all cases distinctly separated from one another by transverse perforated plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of an epistome and presence of transverse perforated partitions between zooecia separate Gymnolæmata from other ectoprocts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheilostomata (suborder) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The zooecia are provided with a 'lip' or lid hinged to the posterior margin of the orifice. This lid closes automatically outside the zooecium or in a special chamber on the external surface (the 'peristome') when the polypide retracts and is pushed open by the tentacles as they expand. Majority of zooecia flattened; presence of vibracula and avicularia in some species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a hinged operculum or lip and often flattened zooecia; note that some freshwater/estuarine occurrences exist though group is essentially marine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ctenostomata (suborder) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Zooecia provided with a collar-like membrane pleated vertically which closes together above the polypide inside the zooecium when retracted and expands into a ring-shaped form before tentacles are extruded. Zooecia usually tubular but sometimes flattened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleated collar (collar-like membrane) that expands into a ring at extension is diagnostic; many are marine but some groups include freshwater genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclostomata (suborder) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Zooecia provided neither with a lip nor with a collar-like membrane. They are tubular and usually have circular orifices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of both lip and collar and tubular zooecia with circular orifices identify cyclostomes; noted as exclusively marine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order PHYLACTOLÆMATA diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Ectoproctous polyzoa the polypides of which have a leaf-shaped organ called an epistome projecting upwards and forwards within the circle of tentacles and between the mouth and the anus. The zooecia are not distinct from one another; in dendritic forms the zoarium is divided irregularly by chitinous partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of an epistome and non-separated zooecia (freshwater exclusivity) are essential; family- and genus-level distinctions follow from details of zoarium partitioning and anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisions of CTENOSTOMATA characters (Alcyonellea, Stolonifera, Vesicularina, Paludicellina)
rubrics_metrics.description: Division I Alcyonellea: zooecia arise directly in a fleshy/gelatinous mass; polypide has no gizzard. Division II Stolonifera: zooecia arise from expansions in a delicate creeping rhizome; usually no gizzard. Division III Vesicularina: zooecia grow from a tubular stem (free/vertical); stout gizzard with internal chitinous projections tightly compressed when polypide retracted. Division IV Paludicellina (nov.): zooecia arranged in regular cruciform manner; if gizzard present it does not bear internal chitinous projections; mostly freshwater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mode of zoarium construction (fleshy mass, creeping rhizome, tubular stem, cruciform arrangement) and gizzard presence/structure to place ctenostomes into these divisions; Paludicellina includes all true freshwater ctenostomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zoarium morphology as diagnostic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole body of zooecia which are in organic connection. Zoarium may be recumbent or erect, formed of zooecia arising directly in cruciform formation or joined by tubular processes; may form tangled masses where true arrangement only recognizable at terminal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrangement of zooecia in the zoarium (cruciform, linear, recumbent, erect, tangled fur-like masses) is a key character at family/genus/species levels; examine growing points to ascertain true pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zooecium structural characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Zooecia may be tubular or flattened; orifice may be terminal, subterminal, or dorsal; orifice shape (angulate, subangulate, quadrate, circular) and presence of stiff ectocyst influence appearance of orifice (e.g., four flaps/valves). Presence/absence of parietal muscles, adventitious buds, and tubules are diagnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record orifice position and shape, ectocyst rigidity, presence of parietal muscles and adventitious buds when distinguishing genera and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polypide anatomical characters (gizzard, tentacles, funiculus, muscles, gonad position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polypide features used diagnostically include presence/absence and form of gizzard (stout, with/without internal chitinous projections), number of tentacles (commonly 8, 16, or 12–20), number and condition of funiculi (one, two, rudimentary or absent), presence of parietal muscles, circular muscles, retractor muscles, and the position of ovaries/testes (on endocyst or funiculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These internal anatomical features (especially gizzard form and funiculus) are critical for separating genera such as Victorella, Paludicella, Hislopia, etc.; examine well-preserved or living material for reliable detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resting buds (hibernacula) characters and phenology
rubrics_metrics.description: Resting buds consist of masses of cells at the base of zooecia, gorged with food material and covered with a resistant horny covering. In Europe/N. America called 'hibernacula' (formed for winter), but in India formed at approach of summer; they germinate when conditions become favourable. Shapes vary (spindle-shaped, flat with marginal projections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence, shape, timing of resting-bud formation and germination are diagnostic and important for life-cycle interpretation; note geographic/seasonal differences (e.g., Indian species form them in hot weather).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gizzard structure and function as a diagnostic and biological character
rubrics_metrics.description: Gizzard may be stout with internal chitinous projections (e.g., Vesicularina) or have a thin membranous sac-like form (Victorella). In Hislopia the gizzard is unique: a tubular portion that can close from oesophagus, a spherical part uniformly lined with thick chitinous layer appearing as ridges, and a ring of powerful cilia at its lower aperture. The gizzard may act as a reservoir holding green cysts (encysted unicellular organisms) and other food items, with muscular contractions periodically forcing contents into the stomach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed gizzard morphology (lining, muscular/glandular layers, ciliation, ability to close) provides high-resolution taxonomic and functional information; observe living material to see ciliary and muscular activity and green cyst contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding evidence from gut/gizzard contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Food of some species (e.g., Victorella bengalensis) consists largely of diatoms (siliceous shells constituting excreta). Hislopia's gizzard contains green cysts (likely encysted flagellates allied to Euglena) which may surrender stored food material to the polyzoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining gut/gizzard contents (diatoms, green cysts) yields ecological and functional inference and can help distinguish species with different feeding/reservoir strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-level key characters within Paludicellidæ (Paludicella, Victorella, Pottsiella)
rubrics_metrics.description: I. Orifice terminal; main axis vertical; zooecia separated by tubules. A. Base of zooecia not swollen; no adventitious buds = Pottsiella. B. Base swollen; adventitious buds near tip = Victorella. II. Orifice subterminal on dorsal surface; main axis horizontal; buds not at tip = Paludicella.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use orifice position (terminal vs subterminal/dorsal), main axis orientation (vertical vs horizontal), presence/absence and position of adventitious buds, and base swelling to assign specimens to these genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family HISLOPIIDÆ diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoarium recumbent, often forming an almost uniform layer; zooecia flattened, adherent, with orifice dorsal either surrounded by a chitinous rim or at tip of erect chitinous tubule; no parietal muscles; polypide with an ample gizzard uniformly lined with chitin; funiculus rudimentary or absent; ovaries and testes not fixed to lateral walls; resting buds not produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flattened, adherent zooecia with a chitin-lined gizzard and absence of parietal muscles strongly indicate Hislopiidae; be cautious of superficial resemblance to cheilostomes in preserved specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misidentification from preserved specimen artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: In preserved material structures (e.g., thickened rim of orifice, enlarged posterior tentacle-fold) may resemble cheilostome peristomes or lips, leading to misplacement (Carter's misidentification of Hislopia as a cheilostome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine living specimens when possible; observe dynamic features (tentacle-fold variability, collar behavior) to avoid errors arising from preservation artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-level diagnostic characters example: Victorella bengalensis
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoarium resembles a thick fur; elongate erect slender tubules as 'hairs'; base often an irregular membrane of matted tubules; zoarium faint yellowish tinge. Young zooecia ovoid with stout quadrate orificial tubule projecting upwards; adventitious buds often given off near orifice and prolific budding at tip producing multi-generation buds; polypide with 8 slender tentacles and a gizzard whose base is surrounded by a strong circular muscle; resting buds flat with marginal projections; habitat brackish pools of Ganges delta and salt lakes near Calcutta; feeds largely on diatoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine zoarium macroscopy (fur-like, colour), orificial shape, adventitious budding pattern, polypide anatomy, resting-bud form and ecology/distribution to distinguish V. bengalensis from similar taxa (e.g., Bowerbankia caudata).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-level diagnostic note example: Bowerbankia caudata subsp. bengalensis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguished from typical B. caudata by greater luxuriance of growth and an often relatively long 'tail' produced below the point of fixation; stem divided at intervals by partitions, crossing and anastomosing to form a fur-like structure with elongated zooecia; zoarium has greenish or greyish tinge. Found commonly in brackish water in the Ganges delta and Chilka Lake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth habit (tail presence/length, luxuriance), stem partitioning/anastomosis, and zoarium coloration are important for subspecific identification in field-collected material.
